strings.title: Typing Zoo
strings.tag: Learn to type, one key at a time, and hatch a pet after every lesson.
strings.how1: Put your fingers on the home row: A S D F for your left hand, J K L ; for your right hand.
strings.how2: Feel the little bumps on F and J. They help you find home without looking.
strings.how3: Type the letter that is lit up. Finish the lesson to crack an egg and hatch a pet.
strings.hello: Pick a lesson. Each one ends with an egg to crack!
strings.locked: Finish the lesson before to open this one.
strings.petsSub: Finish lessons to hatch more. Get 3 stars for a golden egg and a shiny pet!
strings.artCredit: Animal art: Noto Emoji by Google, CC BY 4.0
strings.start: Press Space or tap Start to begin.
strings.shiftHint: Hold Shift with your other hand's pinky for a big letter.
strings.keepGoing: Nice work! Try again for more stars.
strings.eggReady: Your egg is ready! Tap it or press any key to crack it.
strings.noKb: Typing practice works best with a keyboard. You can also tap the keys below.
strings.tickTip: Typed wrong? No problem. Find the lit-up key and try again.
strings.intro_l01: Rest your left pointer finger on F and your right pointer finger on J. Feel the bumps!
strings.intro_l02: Your middle fingers rest on D and K, right next to F and J.
strings.intro_l03: Your ring fingers rest on S and L.
strings.intro_l04: Your pinkies rest on A and the ; key. That is the whole home row!
strings.intro_l05: Now type real words with the home row keys.
strings.intro_l06: Reach your pointer fingers to the middle: G and H. Then come back home.
strings.intro_l07: Reach up from D to E, and up from K to I.
strings.intro_l08: Reach up from F to R, and up from J to U.
strings.intro_l09: Reach up and over to T and Y with your pointer fingers.
strings.intro_l10: Ring fingers reach up to W and O.
strings.intro_l11: Pinkies reach up to Q and P.
strings.intro_l12: Words that use the top row and the home row.
strings.intro_l13: Reach down from F to V, and down from J to M.
strings.intro_l14: Middle fingers reach down to C and the comma.
strings.intro_l15: Pointer fingers reach down to B and N.
strings.intro_l16: Ring fingers reach down to X and the period. Pinkies reach down to Z.
strings.intro_l18: Big letters: hold Shift with one pinky and press the letter with the other hand.
strings.intro_l19: Type whole sentences with big letters and periods.
strings.intro_l20: A speed run! Type carefully first, then get faster.
strings.intro_l29: Type whole paragraphs now. Keep your eyes on the words, not your fingers.
strings.intro_l30: Keep a steady beat. Smooth typing is faster than rushing.
strings.intro_l31: Watch for capital letters on names and places. Use the Shift key on the other hand.
strings.intro_l32: Numbers and words mixed together. Reach up for the number row and come back home.
strings.intro_l33: Quotation marks are Shift and the apostrophe key, with your right pinky.
strings.intro_l34: A full paragraph for speed. Stay relaxed and keep going.
strings.intro_l35: Longer text with harder words. Accuracy first, then speed.
strings.intro_l36: A short history passage. Read a few words ahead as you type.
strings.intro_l37: Instructions with numbers, colons and commas.
strings.intro_l38: A story with dialogue and punctuation. Take your time with each mark.
strings.intro_l39: Semicolons, dashes and apostrophes all in one place.
strings.intro_l40: The final run. Type smoothly, fix mistakes quickly, and finish strong.
strings.intro_l21: Reach up from F to 4, and up from J to 7. Keep your other fingers home.
strings.intro_l22: Pointer fingers stretch to 5 and 6, in the middle of the number row.
strings.intro_l23: Middle fingers reach up to 3 and 8.
strings.intro_l24: Ring fingers reach up to 2 and 9.
strings.intro_l26: Words and numbers together, like 3 cats and 12 dogs.
strings.intro_l27: A question mark is Shift and the / key. An exclamation mark is Shift and 1.
strings.intro_l28: The apostrophe is next to ; and the dash is next to 0. Both use your right pinky.
strings.testsSub: Type as much as you can before the time runs out.
strings.testsLocked: Finish Lesson 12 to open the typing tests.
strings.intro_test: Type as much as you can in {n} minutes. The clock starts with your first key. Fix any mistakes as you go.
strings.intro_tricky: These are the keys you miss most. Go slowly and get each one right.
strings.ownSub: Write a lesson or a timed test with your own words, then share its class code or assign it.
strings.textHint: Letters, numbers, spaces and . , ; : ' " - ! ? ( ). Each line is typed in turn. 10 to 1,500 characters.
strings.codeHow: Students open Typing Zoo and type this code, or you assign it to a class.
strings.delAsk: Delete this lesson? Its class code and links will stop working.
strings.saveErr: That didn't save. Check the text has only keys from the keyboard and nothing personal or unkind.
strings.badChars: These can't be typed in Typing Zoo: {chars}
strings.codeH: Got a code from your teacher?
strings.codeBad: That code doesn't work. Check it with your teacher.
strings.missing: This lesson isn't there anymore. Ask your teacher for a new code.
strings.passNot: Not passed yet. You need {what}. Try again to crack your egg!
strings.needRule: Your teacher asks for {what} in the lesson before to open this one.
strings.ruleNot: To open the next lesson, your teacher asks for {what}. Try this one again!
strings.keyboardHint: Pick the language and keyboard you type on.

sentences: The cat sat on a mat.
We can play in the park.
She has a big blue kite.
My pet is soft and kind.
The moon is bright at night.

paras.l29: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. They can change color in less than a second to hide from fish that want to eat them. An octopus can also squeeze through any gap that is bigger than its beak.
paras.l30: The Moon is about a quarter of the size of Earth. It has no air, so there is no wind to blow away the footprints left by astronauts. Those prints could stay there for millions of years.
paras.l31: Maya and her brother Leo flew from Chicago to Lisbon in June. On Tuesday they rode a yellow tram up a steep hill, and on Friday they visited Aunt Rosa, who lives near the sea in a little blue house.
paras.l32: Our class planted 24 seeds on March 3. After 10 days, 18 of them had sprouted. By the end of April the tallest plant was 35 centimeters tall, and we picked 7 ripe tomatoes in the first week of June.
paras.l33: "Can we go outside?" asked Sam. "Not yet," said Mr. Park. "First, finish your page." Sam typed as fast as he could. "Done!" he called. "Great," said Mr. Park, "now we can all go out and play."
paras.l34: Every morning the baker wakes up before the sun. She mixes flour, water, salt, and yeast, then waits for the dough to rise. By seven o'clock the shop smells of warm bread, and a line of hungry people is waiting at the door.
paras.l35: Plants make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. Their leaves take in sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, and they turn them into sugar and oxygen. The oxygen escapes into the air, which is lucky for every animal that needs to breathe.
paras.l36: Long before paper, people wrote on clay tablets, animal skins, and strips of bamboo. Around two thousand years ago, papermakers in China learned to mash plant fibers in water, spread the pulp on a screen, and dry it in the sun. Paper was cheap, light, and easy to carry.
paras.l37: How to make a paper boat: (1) Fold a sheet in half from top to bottom. (2) Fold the top corners down to the middle. (3) Fold the bottom edges up on both sides. (4) Open the middle and flatten it into a square. (5) Pull the sides out gently, and your boat is ready to sail.
paras.l38: The storm knocked out the lights just as the game began. "Don't worry," said Grandpa, lighting a candle. "We'll play the old way." He found a deck of cards in the drawer, and for three hours nobody missed the screen at all. When the power came back, they kept playing.
paras.l39: It wasn't easy; the trail was steep, muddy, and full of roots. Still, the hikers kept going - one slow step at a time - until they reached the top. "Was it worth it?" asked Jo. Everyone looked at the view and laughed; nobody needed to answer.
paras.l40: Hummingbirds are the smallest birds in the world, yet they are amazing athletes. Their wings can beat more than 50 times a second, and their hearts can beat over 1,000 times a minute. They can fly forward, backward, and even upside down, and each day they visit hundreds of flowers to drink sweet nectar.
